props.title: Personal Services

sections.content: Personal Services stands as Terry Jones' bold exploration of Britain's sex work industry in the Thatcher era, based on the real story of Cynthia Payne. Julie Walters delivers a career-defining performance as Christine Painter, a suburban madam running a brothel for elderly gentlemen. The film exemplifies a uniquely British approach to taboo subjects, using humor and social commentary similar to The Life and Loves of a She-Devil (1986) and Wish You Were Here (1987). Jones, fresh from Monty Python, brings his signature mix of comedy and social satire while exposing class hypocrisies.

sections.content: The late 1980s marked a significant shift in British cinema's treatment of sexuality and class. Personal Services sits alongside films like Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987) and Prick Up Your Ears (1987) in challenging conservative values while maintaining a distinctly British sense of humor. Julie Walters' Christine echoes other strong female leads of the era, like Miranda Richardson in Dance with a Stranger (1985), portraying complex women navigating social restrictions and moral judgments. SUBHEAD: Social Commentary in Thatcher's Britain

The film's timing during Thatcher's government wasn't coincidental. Like My Beautiful Laundrette (1985) and Business as Usual (1987), Personal Services used comedy to critique social inequality and conservative morality. The elderly clients - many representing the establishment - highlight the hypocrisy of those condemning sex work while secretly participating in it. This theme of double standards appears in later films like The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover (1989).
